title: S723 Final Simulation Program
agent: Agent T — S723 Governance Closure Program
scope: Full governance simulation — routine maintenance, DCS adjudication, anomaly detection
methodology: Walked each scenario against the S723 governance documentation (MAINTENANCE_FRAMEWORK.json, OPERATIONAL_READINESS.json, CLOSURE_BASELINE.json, DIFFICULTY_GOVERNANCE_AUDIT.json, COGNITIVELEVEL_AUDIT.json, DCS_CERTIFICATION_AUDIT.json) with cross-reference to AGENTS.md §9-13, CURRENT_BASELINES.md, DEFECT_LIBRARY.md, and CAQS_v1.0.md §6.

scenario_1_routine_maintenance.simulation: A new session operator — first day, no prior knowledge of the project — opens the repository and follows the AGENTS.md §9 Session Startup Protocol. They: (1) Read SESSION_STATUS_2026-07-24.md §6 and see '2,031 certified' — but this is stale, the actual is 2,181 per CURRENT_BASELINES.md. (2) Read REVISION_HISTORY.md latest entries and see S802/S722A activity. (3) Run governance guard test suite: 20/20 PASS. (4) Run certified-count grep per AGENTS.md §9.3: result is 2,181 — this contradicts the stale SESSION_STATUS number they read in step 1, causing confusion. (5) They check AGENTS.md §9.2 which says '~1,080 certified' — a third conflicting number. The operator now faces 3 different certified counts from 3 governance documents. (6) They check CognitiveLevel coverage: 100% — all 2,500 items carry a valid CL field. (7) They check difficulty distribution and see Moderate at 48.4%, Easy+Moderate-Easy at 48.1%, Difficult at 3.5%, Very Difficult at 0%. The distribution is severely skewed but their reading of CAQS §6.1 targets gives them the reference point to recognize this. (8) They check CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 and see 'DL-008: 67 Certified items (CRITICAL)' — the document reports a severe learner-safety risk.
detected_issues: DOCUMENT_STALENESS: AGENTS.md §9.2 says '~1,080 certified' — actual is 2,181. First number the operator sees is wrong by ~1,100 items (51% undercount). This is a CRITICAL documentation defect per COND-1 of the operational readiness audit.

STALE_SESSION_STATUS: SESSION_STATUS_2026-07-24.md reports 2,031 certified — actual is 2,181 (7% undercount). The operator must choose between 3 contradictory authoritative numbers: AGENTS.md (~1,080), SESSION_STATUS (2,031), grep result (2,181).
DIFFICULTY_DISTRIBUTION_SKEW: 0 Very Difficult items in a 2,500-item pool (CAQS target: 10%). The operator would detect this immediately if they compare the distribution to CAQS §6.1 targets.

COGNITIVELEVEL_DISTRIBUTION_GAP: 0 Evaluate items, only 10 Analyze items (0.40%). The operator would see the CAQS §6.2 target says 15% Evaluate (375 items) and 25% Analyze (625 items). Extreme noncompliance is obvious.

CURRENT_BASELINES_STALE_DL008: The baseline document reports 67 Certified DL-008 items as CRITICAL — but S801/S802 refuted these as DL-029 scan artifacts. The operator would see a CRITICAL alert in the baseline document and not know whether to trust it or the S802 refutation.

GOVERNANCE_GUARD_METHOD_GAP: The operator runs the governance guard and gets 20/20 PASS. They do NOT realize the guard's DL-008 detection uses the same ±1200-char window scan method that the project proved produces ~75% false positives (DL-029). A pass here is misleading — it doesn't mean DL-008-free, it means DL-029-limited scanning found nothing in its unreliable window.
missed_issues: P1-CC-050 DL-008 SURVIVOR: One confirmed Certified DL-008 item (Pack C Section C, CC=C, EW-C non-empty with variance analysis text). The operator's grep of question_state='Certified' and governance guard test would NOT detect this. The guard's window-scan method specifically missed it (DL-029 vulnerability). Only a boundary-aware Function-constructor parse with direct EW[CC] extraction would catch it. The operator has no instruction to perform this scan — the maintenance framework puts DL-008 boundary-aware re-scan at MONTHLY frequency (M3), not weekly.

DL-016 METADATA-CONTENT MISMATCH: Affects ALL Pack A sections. Metadata-block ChoiceA-D differs from content-block Choices.A-D, meaning EW text may describe the wrong item's distractors. The operator's CL coverage check and governance guard test would NOT detect this — no automated check exists for cross-block content consistency. The operator has no instruction to scan for this.

DL-013 BOILERPLATE (851 FIELDS): The operator's CL/distribution checks wouldn't surface explanation quality issues. Boilerplate text ('represents a plausible misconception...') degrades educational value but the operator has no check in the weekly W1-W3 schedule for explanation quality.

129 LABEL-SCORE MISMATCHES: Difficulty (string) doesn't match DifficultyScore (integer) for 129 items. The operator running a Difficulty distribution check might flag the skew but wouldn't detect individual mismatches without per-item field extraction.
174 SEVERE DCS §3 VIOLATIONS: 171 Apply@Easy items + 4 Analyze@DS1 items. The operator's surface-level distribution check wouldn't identify individual CL-DS-implausibility pairs.
stability_failure_modes: MODE 1 — DOCUMENT TRAUMA: The operator's first 3 governance numbers (AGENTS.md: ~1,080, SESSION_STATUS: 2,031, grep: 2,181) are all different. They cannot determine which is authoritative without reading CURRENT_BASELINES.md §2 — but AGENTS.md §9.1 tells them to trust SESSION_STATUS. The operator must independently discover that all prior guidance was stale. This is not 'routine' — it requires forensic document reconciliation before any check can be trusted.

MODE 2 — SCAN METHOD DISCONNECT: The governance guard reports 20/20 PASS, suggesting all enforcement rules are satisfied. But the guard's DL-008 detection method is DL-029-vulnerable. The operator has no way to know the guard's pass is unreliable for its own most critical rule. The project proved ±1200-char window scanning is ~75% false-positive prone (S801/S802) but never fixed the guard itself (COND-4). This creates a false sense of security — the operator believes DL-008 is clean when it may not be.

MODE 3 — FREQUENCY GAP: The weekly operator checks do not include hash verification (that's monthly M1). If an unauthorized pack file modification occurred between sessions, the certified-count grep might still return 2,181 (if the modification was metadata-only or a swap of equivalent items), but the hash would differ. The operator would not detect this for up to 30 days. This is a coverage gap in the audit cadence design.

NET EFFECT: A diligent first-day operator would correctly identify 6 surface-level issues (distribution skew, CL gaps, document staleness) but would completely miss P1-CC-050 — the one actual learner-safety defect — because the tools they were told to trust (governance guard, certified-count grep) can't detect it and the scan that would detect it (boundary-aware DL-008 audit) is scheduled monthly, not at onboarding.
recommendations: P0 (CRITICAL): Fix AGENTS.md §9.1-9.3 to reference CURRENT_BASELINES.md as the authoritative source for all counts and to remove the hardcoded '~1,080' stale number. The first action any new operator takes should give them the correct baseline.

P0 (CRITICAL): Generate fresh SESSION_STATUS as part of every maintenance audit. The current file is 2 days stale and contradicted by ground truth. A stale status document is worse than no status document.

P1 (HIGH): Fix governance guard DL-008 detection to use Function-constructor parse instead of the ±1200-char window (per S802's 8 permanent prevention rules and COND-4). The guard cannot enforce Rule 2 using a method the project itself proved unreliable.

P1 (HIGH): Add hash verification to the WEEKLY W1-W3 schedule. Currently only covered at MONTHLY M1. Hash drift is the single most reliable signal that something changed — withholding it from weekly checks creates a detection gap of up to 30 days.

P2 (MEDIUM): Add a T0 automated checklist script that reads CURRENT_BASELINES.md, computes hashes, verifies certified count, and cross-checks key governance documents for staleness. This would have caught the AGENTS.md/SESSION_STATUS staleness before the operator relied on it.

P2 (MEDIUM): Resolve the CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 DL-008 CRITICAL entry. It reports 67 Certified items that S801/S802 proved are scan artifacts. The operator's first encounter with the baseline document shows a CRITICAL risk that doesn't exist — eroding trust in the entire baseline.

scenario_2_dcs_adjudication.simulation: A new calculation question is proposed for certification: 'A company has the following standard costs: direct materials $12/unit, direct labor $8/unit, variable overhead $5/unit, fixed overhead $4/unit. Actual production was 10,000 units. What is the total standard cost of production?' The question requires applying given standard cost rates to a given production volume — a formula-application calculation with the method provided in the stem. Two reviewers independently classify it using the DCS v1.1 framework. Reviewer 1 classifies it as Apply/Moderate (3). Reviewer 2 classifies it as Understand/Moderate-Easy (2), arguing the operativity test fails because the scenario is 'cosmetic wrapper' — the company name and production numbers are template fill, and the question really tests whether the candidate multiplies five numbers together and adds them. They disagree.
scenario_2_dcs_adjudication.decision_path: STEP 1 — Read the stem: 'A company has the following standard costs... Actual production was 10,000 units. What is the total standard cost of production?' Identify the cognitive process required: the candidate must (a) identify that total standard cost = Σ(standard rate × actual quantity) for each cost element, (b) multiply each standard rate by 10,000, (c) sum the five products. STEP 2 — Apply the boundary trees. §9.1 Remember vs Understand — Same-Domain Distractor Test: the distractors would be different total-cost figures (requiring understanding of which elements to include). If distractors span different domains → Remember; otherwise Understand. For a well-written calculation question, distractors are domain-consistent (all cost management). Verdict: at minimum Understand. §9.2 Understand vs Apply — Scenario Operativity Test: The stem has a company context ('A company...'), production volume (10,000 units), and five distinct cost elements. The operativity test asks: are operative facts required to solve? Yes — the candidate must use 10,000 units (not any other figure) and the specific standard rates ($12, $8, $5, $4). The method (multiply and sum) is given — this falls under the method-given supplemental test. Per §9.2, when the method IS given but operative facts are required, classification is Apply. §9.3 Apply vs Analyze — Method-Selection Test: The method (multiply and sum) is directly given in the fact pattern. The candidate does not select a method from competing alternatives. Verdict: Apply, not Analyze. STEP 3 — Assign CL→Difficulty default per DCS §3: Apply → Moderate (DifficultyScore 3, label 'Moderate'). STEP 4 — Apply pre-certification checklist §10: boundary zone tests = PASS (Apply), forbidden triggers = none triggered ('most appropriate' not in stem, company name not cosmetic-only, no template rotation, CL confidence assigned by reviewer). STEP 5 — Final classification: CognitiveLevel = Apply, Difficulty = Moderate, DifficultyScore = 3.
scenario_2_dcs_adjudication.reviewer_1_path: Reviewer 1 classifies as Apply → Moderate (3). Reasoning: (a) Operative facts required — 10,000 units, $12, $8, $5, $4 are all operative; (b) method given — multiply and sum; (c) candidate executes a procedure (multiplication and addition) — fits Apply per Bloom's. Confidence: 90/100.
scenario_2_dcs_adjudication.reviewer_2_path: Reviewer 2 classifies as Understand → Moderate-Easy (2). Reasoning: (a) The company context is cosmetic — 'A company has the following standard costs...' is template text; (b) the operativity test fails because the calculation is trivial — any candidate who knows standard costing multiplies rates by volume; (c) the real cognitive demand is understanding what 'total standard cost' means conceptually, not executing the arithmetic; (d) the question is definition-match adjacent — 'What is standard cost?' → 'sum of standard rates × volume'. (e) Per §8.2 DL-031 pattern: 'Company name in stem ≠ Apply (cosmetic wrapper)'. Confidence: 75/100.
scenario_2_dcs_adjudication.disagreement_analysis: The disagreement is at the Understand-vs-Apply boundary — the HIGHEST disagreement zone documented in DCS v1.1 §11.4 with a baseline agreement rate of 73.7% and an Apply→Understand hotspot rate of 86.3%. Reviewer 1 applies the §9.2 operativity test at face value: operative facts are present → Apply. Reviewer 2 applies the §8.2 forbidden trigger: cosmetic company name + trivial arithmetic = definition-match pattern → Understand. Both are using DCS tools correctly. The conflict arises because §9.2 (the operativity test for Understand vs Apply) and §8.2 (the forbidden trigger 'cosmetic company name') can produce divergent outcomes on edge cases where the question has genuine operative facts (numeric data) but those facts are trivially applied. The DCS v1.1 framework does not have a rule for resolving boundary conflicts between §9 (decision trees) and §8 (forbidden triggers) when they point to different classifications.
scenario_2_dcs_adjudication.disagreement_resolution: Per DCS v1.1 §11.1 — Disagreement Resolution Process: Step 1: A third independent reviewer is assigned. The third reviewer reads the stem, derives the correct answer independently, then classifies using the DCS decision trees without seeing either prior classification. Step 2: The third reviewer's classification is compared against reviewers 1 and 2. If the third reviewer agrees with either reviewer 1 or 2, that forms a 2-of-3 majority — the majority classification is adopted. The dissenting reviewer's opinion is recorded per §11.3 documentation standard. Step 3: If the third reviewer produces a DIFFERENT classification from both reviewers 1 and 2 (a 3-way split), per §11.5: the item enters the Editorial Queue. Certification is blocked. The item must be escalated to human-tiebreak — a human reviewer makes the final CL determination. The DCS amendment conditions (C3, C5) are relevant here: C3 (multi-level tree chaining) means the third reviewer must explicitly walk through all 4 boundary trees starting from §9.1, not assume prior reviewers' starting points. C5 (human-tiebreak undefined) means if it reaches human escalation, the process is underspecified — who, turnaround time, and unavailability fallback are not defined.

gap_details.description: §9.2 operativity test and §8.2 forbidden triggers can produce divergent outcomes on calculation questions with trivial arithmetic but genuine operative data. When a forbidden trigger says 'cosmetic wrapper → Understand' but the decision tree says 'operative facts present → Apply', there is no priority rule. Both are correct applications of their respective DCS sections. The standard needs an explicit override rule: 'Decision trees (§9) take precedence over generic forbidden triggers (§8) when the question provides operative numeric data. Forbidden triggers should be used to exclude classifications that contradict clear evidence, not override decision trees that produce a classification consistent with the evidence.'
gap_details.resolution: The third-reviewer process would likely produce a 2-of-3 majority (most third reviewers, applying the §9.2 operativity test strictly, would side with Reviewer 1 = Apply). But the process itself is fragile — it depends on the third reviewer's interpretation of an unranked conflict between §9 and §8. With DCS reliability at 95.0%, the probability of the third reviewer adding confusion rather than breaking the tie is 5%. For a production system in maintenance mode, this boundary should be explicitly defined.

gap_details.description: Reviewer 2's confidence of 75/100 triggers two different rules depending on which DCS section is consulted. §10 pre-certification checklist says 'CL confidence ≥70 or human-reviewed' — Reviewer 2's classification would be auto-accepted at 75. But §13.1 confidence gate protocol says 70-84 = 'Accept with rationale: The classifier must provide specific justification for the CL assignment.' Under §13.1, Reviewer 2's 75 classification IS acceptable but requires documented rationale — which Reviewer 2 has provided (cosmetic wrapper argument). The C1 contradiction is that §10 implies auto-accept at any ≥70 — no rationale needed — while §13.1 requires rationale at 70-84. If this item enters the pre-certification checklist under §10 alone, Reviewer 2's classification might be accepted without rationale documentation. If §13.1 governs, the rationale is required but the classification still counts. The resolution recommended by CAPA-DCS-002 (make §13.1 authoritative, raise the gate to 85 for auto-accept) would make Reviewer 2's classification require rationale — which Reviewer 2 has provided — so the classification stands but is properly documented. Net effect: the C1 contradiction creates procedural uncertainty but in this scenario, Reviewer 2's classification with rationale is acceptable under either rule. However, the operator running the DCS checklist must know WHICH confidence threshold applies.

If the three reviewers produce a true 3-way split (no majority), the escalation path per §11.2/§11.5 is: 'Escalate to human-tiebreak.' But §11.2 does not specify who the human is, what turnaround time is expected, or what happens if the human is unavailable. The item sits in the Editorial Queue indefinitely. For a single question in a production maintenance mode, this is acceptable — the item is excluded from the learner pool until resolved. For a batch of 30+ contentious items, the indefinite queue creates a governance backlog that never auto-resolves.

scenario_2_dcs_adjudication.dcs_note: For straightforward calculation questions — where the method is given, operative facts are unambiguous, and no forbidden triggers apply — DCS v1.1 produces deterministic, replicable outcomes. Both reviewers in this scenario would produce the same classification for a clearly operative calculation (e.g., standard costing variance breakdown, cash collections with multi-step percentage application, learning curve calculation with given exponent). The disagreement only emerges at the boundary zone where calculation triviality and cosmetic context interact. The 95.0% reliability rate (S722A) confirms that 19 of 20 classifications are consistent. The 1-in-20 disagreement rate maps almost entirely to Understand-vs-Apply boundary cases.

scenario_3_anomaly_detection.simulation: A routine weekly maintenance session opens. The operator runs W1 (governance guard: 20/20 PASS), W2 (certified count: 2,181 — matches CURRENT_BASELINES.md, stable), W3 (defect library: no new entries since last session). All weekly checks pass. Unbeknownst to the operator, a concurrent session 12 hours earlier performed a metadata-only fix on pack_c_corrected.js — it filled a missing Difficulty field on P1-CD-050 and updated the DifficultyScore from 3 to 4 on two items (P1-CD-072, P1-CD-073) without documenting in REVISION_HISTORY.md (a governance guard Rule 1 and Rule 4 violation — but the concurrent session operator overrode the guard's WARN because 'it's just metadata, not content'). The file hash of pack_c_corrected.js has changed. The certified count is still 350 (Pack C). The parse-count is still 500. The governance guard test suite still passes (the guard doesn't check hashes).
scenario_3_anomaly_detection.escalation_path: CURRENT PATH (what happens today): The operator completes W1-W3 checks. All pass. The operator logs a session-closing REVISION_HISTORY.md entry: 'Weekly maintenance audit — all checks pass. Certified count: 2,181. Governance guard: 20/20 PASS. No new defects.' The operator does NOT detect the hash drift because hash verification is in the MONTHLY M1 check, not the weekly W1-W3. The unauthorized metadata change goes undetected for up to 30 days until the next monthly audit. If the monthly audit is missed or delayed (operator thinks 'everything passed weekly, monthly will be fine'), the hash drift could persist indefinitely.
scenario_3_anomaly_detection.intended_path_per_framework: Per the maintenance framework §audit_cadence → ad_hoc_triggers: 'Any pack file modification (content or metadata)' triggers full hash recomputation, parse-count verification, DL-008 boundary-aware re-scan, REVISION_HISTORY entry, and CURRENT_BASELINES update. Per the escalation playbook §level_3: 'Hash drift on any pack file without documented write session in REVISION_HISTORY.md → CRITICAL → IMMEDIATE EXIT from maintenance mode, Level 3 escalation.' Per trigger threshold 'hash_drift': 'Any protected file SHA-256 mismatch vs. CURRENT_BASELINES.md §1 without a documented write session → Level 3 escalation — IMMEDIATE EXIT. Unauthorized file modification.' The PLAYBOOK IS CORRECT — it defines the right response. The issue is not the playbook's content but its activation cadence: the hash check that would trigger the playbook happens at MONTHLY (M1), not WEEKLY. An unauthorized change made on Day 1 may not be detected until Day 30.
why_not_caught: FREQUENCY_GAP: The maintenance framework's weekly W1-W3 checks do not include hash verification. Hash verification is scheduled at MONTHLY M1. An unauthorized file change is a level-3-critical event but the detection mechanism operates at a monthly cadence. The gap between 'detection cadence' (monthly) and 'severity of the trigger' (critical, immediate) is misaligned — critical events need immediate detection, not monthly-batched detection.

GOVERNANCE_GUARD_SCOPE_LIMITATION: The governance guard test suite (20 tests) uses synthetic test strings — it does not load actual pack files. The guard would not flag the metadata change because its DL-008 detection didn't find new violations (the metadata fix didn't touch ExplanationWrong fields) and its Rule 1/4 WARN checks are not invoked during the test suite (they fire at session idle based on REVISION_HISTORY.md cross-references, not file-hash changes).

CERTIFIED_COUNT_STABILITY_AS_FALSE_REASSURANCE: W2 reported certified count stable at 2,181. An unauthorized metadata-only change (Difficulty label, DifficultyScore) doesn't change question_state, so W2 correctly reports stability. But W2 stability can be misinterpreted as 'nothing changed' when in fact content metadata changed without authorization. The operator is told in the maintenance framework that 'certified count change = Level 3 escalation' — implying that NO certified count change = safe. This is a false-equivalence trap.

NO AUTOMATED PRE-SCAN HASH CHECK: The maintenance framework does not have an automated T0 hash verification script that runs at session start (COND-5 gap). The operator must manually compute SHA-256 hashes against CURRENT_BASELINES.md. A manual process that happens monthly is a single point of failure — if the operator skips it (because 'weekly checks were clean'), no automated fallback detects the drift.
scenario_3_anomaly_detection.would_be_caught_eventually: YES — at the monthly M1 audit (≤30 days later). The hash verification would flag the mismatch. The operator would consult CURRENT_BASELINES.md §1, find the pack_c hash doesn't match, check REVISION_HISTORY.md for a documented write session, find none, and trigger Level 3 escalation per the playbook. Then G1-G5 reconciliation would identify: (1) G1 hash confirmation — pack_c hash changed; (2) G2 parse integrity — still 500 items, no structural corruption; (3) G3 content integrity — CorrectChoice values unchanged, only Difficulty/DifficultyScore fields modified; (4) G4 registry integrity — MASTER_QUESTION_REGISTRY.md QuestionIDs match; (5) G5 certification integrity — certified count unchanged. The investigation would find the unauthorized metadata fix, determine it was a governance guard bypass (the concurrent operator ignored Rule 1/4 WARNs), and the remediation would be: document the change in REVISION_HISTORY.md retroactively, update CURRENT_BASELINES.md with the new hash, and log a new DL-ID documenting the governance guard bypass (per the 'new defect discovery' ad-hoc trigger).

gap_details.description: Critical events (hash drift on pack files) are detected at monthly cadence. The maintenance framework's severity hierarchy says this is a Level 3 CRITICAL event requiring IMMEDIATE exit. But 'immediate' means 0-24 hours, while 'monthly' means up to 30 days. The cadence and severity are procedurally incompatible. An unauthorized change could propagate for 29 days before detection.
gap_details.fix: Add hash verification to the WEEKLY W1-W4 checks. The cost is low (SHA-256 of 15 files takes ~2 seconds). The benefit is detection of unauthorized modification within 7 days instead of 30. If compute time is a concern, limit weekly hash checks to the 5 pack files (the highest-risk targets) and keep full 15-file verification at monthly.

gap_details.description: The maintenance framework's detection model is entirely pull-based (operator runs checks on a schedule). There is no push-trigger mechanism — e.g., a file-system watcher that logs all pack-file modifications, or a git pre-commit hook that enforces hash-recomputation and REVISION_HISTORY entry. Every detection gap in the framework arises from the same source: if the operator doesn't run a check at the right time, the event goes undetected.
gap_details.fix: Consider a git pre-commit hook or file-system watcher that writes a modification log to reports/file_modification_log.json. The weekly operator can then read this log and cross-reference against REVISION_HISTORY.md entries — any modification without a corresponding revision entry is flagged immediately regardless of hash state.

gap_details.description: The maintenance framework's trigger thresholds emphasize certified count stability as the primary integrity metric (Level 3 escalation for any count change). But certified count is stable for metadata-only changes, content swaps where certified-for-certified items are exchanged, and DL-016 dual-block edits where only the metadata block changes. The framework implicitly treats 'certified count unchanged = safe' when this is not true.
gap_details.fix: Add a SECOND integrity metric to the weekly checks: pack file hash verification. The combination of 'certified count stable AND hash stable' is a much stronger integrity signal than either alone. Document in the maintenance framework that certified count alone is insufficient for integrity verification.

gap_details.description: The concurrent session operator overrode governance guard Rule 4 (answer-key WARN) for a metadata change because 'it's just metadata.' Rule 4 triggers on answer-key changes (CorrectChoice, Correct values) — not Difficulty/DifficultyScore. So the override may have been technically correct (Rule 4 didn't fire for metadata). But the operator also failed to create a REVISION_HISTORY.md entry (Rule 1 violation: question_state changes pair with revision entries — and Difficulty changes are content metadata changes per AGENTS.md §4). The failure mode is: operators can rationalize bypassing WARN rules because they're 'just warnings' — the maintenance framework's distinction between BLOCK (hard stop) and WARN (advisory) creates an enforcement gap where WARN rules can be ignored without preventing the session from completing.
gap_details.fix: Document in AGENTS.md §9 (Session Startup Protocol) that WARN-level governance guard triggers must be resolved with a REVISION_HISTORY.md entry before closing ANY session, even if the WARN doesn't block the technical operation. Add to the weekly W3 check: 'Review REVISION_HISTORY.md for any entries referencing governance guard WARN overrides and confirm each has documented rationale.'

overall_stability_assessment.rationale: The 700-series governance closure program has produced a comprehensive, well-intentioned maintenance framework with tiered audits, clear escalation paths, and a detailed trigger-threshold matrix. The framework DESIGN is stable — it correctly identifies what should be checked, how often, and what to do when violations are found. The DCS v1.1 calibration standard is functionally operational with 95.0% reliability. The governance guard provides automated enforcement for 5 rules. However, the simulation reveals 3 structural failure modes that prevent stable autonomous operation:
failure_modes: FAILURE MODE 1 — TRUSTED DOCUMENTS ARE STALE: AGENTS.md §9 directs new operators to stale numbers (~1,080 vs actual 2,181). SESSION_STATUS is 2 days stale (2,031 vs 2,181). CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 reports a CRITICAL risk (67 Certified DL-008) that was proven false by S801/S802. The 3 most-trusted governance documents contain contradictory or refuted information. An operator without 700-series context cannot distinguish authoritative from stale — they will either trust the wrong numbers or lose confidence in all governance documentation. Either outcome destabilizes the maintenance process.

FAILURE MODE 2 — THE GUARD CANNOT DETECT WHAT IT GUARDS AGAINST: Governance guard Rule 2 (BLOCK) enforces DL-008 prevention using a ±1200-char window scan that the project itself proved produces ~75% false positives (DL-029). The one confirmed Certified DL-008 survivor (P1-CC-050) escaped detection by this scan method. A 20/20 PASS on the governance guard test suite does not mean DL-008 is clean — it means the DL-029-vulnerable scan method found nothing in its unreliable window. The project documented the method flaw in its own defect library but never applied the fix to its own enforcement tool. This is a self-correcting failure — the framework learned the right lesson but didn't implement it in its most critical component.

FAILURE MODE 3 — DETECTION CADENCE DOESN'T MATCH SEVERITY: Hash drift on pack files is a Level 3 CRITICAL event requiring IMMEDIATE exit from maintenance mode. But hash verification is scheduled at MONTHLY cadence (M1). Between detection (monthly) and required response time (immediate), there's a 30-day operational gap. A malicious or erroneous file modification could persist for 29 days undetected. The weekly operator checks (W1-W3) cannot detect hash drift — the only signal they validate is certified count stability, which remains unchanged for metadata-only modifications.

FAILURE MODE 4 — DOCUMENTS WITHOUT GUARDIANS: CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 (Defect & Risk Status) was not updated after S801/S802 refuted the 67 Certified DL-008 items. No automated check verifies that CURRENT_BASELINES defect status matches DEFECT_LIBRARY status. REVISION_HISTORY.md is a 1MB single file (16,750 lines) with no automated backup. AGENTS.md has a hardcoded certified count ('~1,080') that diverged from reality months ago. These are all single-points-of-failure with no automated staleness detection.

conditions.description: Before maintenance mode can operate without active oversight, the governance documents that a new operator first reads MUST be accurate. This means: (a) AGENTS.md §9 certified count updated to reference CURRENT_BASELINES.md dynamically (not a hardcoded ~1,080); (b) SESSION_STATUS regenerated to match actual state; (c) CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 updated to remove the refuted 67 Certified DL-008 CRITICAL alert; (d) A mechanism established so these three documents cannot go out of sync — either an automated cross-document consistency script or a 'single-source-of-truth' document that the others reference.

Governance guard Rule 2 DL-008 detection must use boundary-aware Function-constructor parse instead of the ±1200-char window scan. The project has already implemented this method in its scan scripts (S801/S802). The fix is to replace the guard's DL-008 detection logic with a call to the authoritative parser. Until this is done, the governance guard's 20/20 PASS is a misleading signal — it cannot be trusted as evidence that the learner pool is DL-008-free.

conditions.condition: COND-C — ALIGN DETECTION CADENCE WITH SEVERITY
conditions.description: Hash verification (the only check that detects unauthorized file modification) must be added to the weekly audit cadence. Either (a) add M1 hash verification as W4 in the weekly schedule, or (b) add a 'quick hash' of the 5 pack files to weekly and keep full 15-file verification at monthly. The cost of computing 5 SHA-256 hashes is trivial — seconds, not minutes. The detection gap of 30 days is not acceptable for events classified as Level 3 CRITICAL requiring IMMEDIATE response.

Create a T0 baseline verification script (scripts/t0_baseline_verify.js) that runs at every session start per COND-5 of the operational readiness audit. The script must: (a) compute SHA-256 of all protected files and compare against CURRENT_BASELINES.md; (b) grep certified count and compare against CURRENT_BASELINES.md §2; (c) cross-check CURRENT_BASELINES.md §3 defect severity against DEFECT_LIBRARY.md statuses; (d) verify AGENTS.md referenced files exist at their pinned locations; (e) warn if SESSION_STATUS is > 7 days old. This eliminates the single-point-of-failure reliance on manual hash comparison.

conditions.condition: COND-E — RESOLVE THE P1-CC-050 DL-008 SURVIVOR
conditions.description: One confirmed Certified DL-008 item exists in the learner pool (P1-CC-050, Pack C Section C, CC=C, EW-C non-empty with variance analysis text). This is a learner-safety risk — wrong-answer feedback may appear in the correct-answer explanation slot. The fix is a single-item EW[C] clear (the ExplanationCorrect independently contains the full explanation). This should be remediated before any claim of 'maintenance mode stable' is made, because the entire point of maintenance mode is that the learner pool is safe — and it currently has one confirmed unsafe item.

what_works_well: The maintenance framework DESIGN is thorough — 4 audit cadences (weekly/monthly/quarterly/annual), 6 trigger thresholds, 3 escalation levels, ad-hoc triggers for 6 event types. The architecture is correct even if the implementation has gaps.

DCS v1.1 produces deterministic difficulty/CL classifications for 95% of items. For simple calculation questions, the decision trees are unambiguous. For boundary-zone disagreements, the 3-reviewer majority-rule process resolves most disputes. The framework handles the normal case well.
The G1-G5 reconciliation runbook (Session 31) is the correct escalation response for critical events. If a Level 3 escalation IS triggered, the response path is well-defined and comprehensive.

The defect library's learning loop is genuine — DL-019 led to BACKUP_PROTOCOL.md, DL-020 led to string-aware parsers, DL-029 led to 8 prevention rules. The system learns from its failures. The remaining gap is that it hasn't fully applied those lessons to its own enforcement tools.

Certified count stability as a primary integrity metric is well-placed — for content-level changes (question_state, CorrectChoice, ExplanationCorrect), a grep of 'question_state: Certified' would indeed change and trigger W2. The limitation is only for metadata-only changes.
minimum_viable_conditions_for_maintenanc: COND-A (Trusted Documents) — without this, every new operator starts with wrong information
COND-B (Fix the Guard) — without this, the sole automated enforcement tool is unreliable
COND-E (P1-CC-050) — without this, the learner pool has a confirmed safety defect
nice_to_have_conditions_for_maintenance_: COND-C (Detection Cadence) — adds immediate detection for unauthorized modifications

cross_scenario_synthesis.description: The three scenarios expose a common root cause: the 700-series governance closure program produced an excellent set of rules, decision trees, escalation paths, and audit cadences — but the IMPLEMENTATION of those rules (the governance guard plugin, the current state of governance documents, the detection cadence alignment) has not kept pace with the DESIGN. The gap between 'what the framework says should happen' and 'what actually happens when an operator follows it' is the primary source of instability.
key_pattern: The governance guard says 'BLOCK DL-008 certification' but scans using a method the project proved unreliable → enforcement gap
AGENTS.md says 'verify certified count via grep' but also says 'read ~1,080 certified in past state' → reference gap
The maintenance framework says 'hash drift = Level 3 CRITICAL, immediate exit' but schedules hash checks at monthly → cadence gap
DCS v1.1 says 'deterministic boundary trees' but §9 and §8 can conflict on trivial-calculation questions → priority gap
CURRENT_BASELINES.md says '67 Certified DL-008 (CRITICAL)' but S801/S802 proved 0-1 actual → synchronization gap
The pattern is consistent: the FRAMEWORK defines the right thing, but the TOOLS and DATA the operator uses to execute the framework are unreliable, stale, or misaligned.
